text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Prime Minister John Howard yesterday announced the establishment of a pilot work scheme for unemployed young people, which will see them work for the dole, in a bid to tackle Australia's unemployment rate. The move comes ahead of the release this week of labour force figures, expected to show that only 10,000 new jobs were created in January. Page 1.

Telstra will today launch the SureLink electronic payment service - a secure payments system hailed to be as advanced as any in the world - which is expect to help realise the huge potential of the Internet. The key feature of the service is that customer can buy goods and services over the Internet and not have to release credit card and personal details. Page 1.

Prime Minister John Howard has been briefed on an investigation being conducted into National Party MP Michael Cobb's alleged misuse of entitlements and said that although he expected members of his ministry to behave properly, he did not sit in judgement on them. Page 3.

The U.S. Government is pressuring the Federal Government to overturn a Cabinet decision and boost the protection of confidential data used in testing new chemicals and pharmaceuticals. The U.S. has threatened trade sanctions against Australian unless the Cabinet decision is reversed. Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Under a new plan by Prime Minister John Howard, unemployed 16 to 20-year-olds will work up to 20 hours a week on community-based projects. The controversial scheme will be set out in the May budget along with other young unemployment initiatives endorsed last week by the Employment Committee of Cabinet. Page 1.

Prime Minister John Howard's wish that live telecasts of the Australia-South Africa cricket Tests be screened on free-to-air television has seen the Federal Government, Foxtel, News Limited and the Seven Network locked in last minute talks. Page 1.

Yesterday former Prime Minister Gough Whitlam was officially handed his emperor's wreath by an adoring Labor party faithful crowd, ensuring his place in ALP and union history. The former Prime Minister made a speech on the 30th anniversary of his election as Labor leader and was honoured with an annual lecture series in his name. Page 1.

A hardline call by the National Party for legislation to extinguish native title has prompted Prime Minister John Howard to deny any rift in the Coalition Government over the response to the Wik decision. Howard said he understood concerns in rural areas sparked by the decision and claims the National Party had an obligation to represent its constituents. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Police are tracking suspected criminals with mobile telephones to within several hundred metres, angering the NSW Privacy Committee and the NSW Council for Civil Liberties who claim the action is an invasion of privacy and an attack on people's rights. Page 1.

In an attempt to cut unemployment rates, the Federal Government plans to introduce a scheme which will see unemployed youths working up to 20 hours a week in return for the dole. The government will give the Department of Social Security permission to deny benefits to young people who refuse to take pilot programme in rural and regional areas. Page 1.

The Federal Government's strong lobbying of News Ltd and the Seven network may see at least partial live coverage of the cricket Tests and one-day games between Australia and South Africa. The Government has argued for renegotiation of a deal which would have seen only replayed highlights on Seven and live coverage restricted to pay-TV. Page 1.

NSW Health Minister Andrew Refshauge has shown he will not tolerate health managers who fail to pay their bills on time, by issuing a deadline of close of business today for hospitals to pay nearly A$10 million in overdue debts. Page 3.
THE AGE

Confidential incident reports filed by protection workers obtained by The Age have revealed that prostitution, drug-taking and substance abuse by children in state-care is rampant. Human Services Department assistant director of protection and care Penny Armytage admits that some State wards have behavioural problems but says there is little protection workers can do to control them. Page 1.

One of the world's leading classical pianists, Australian Geoffrey Tozer, has decided to permanently move to Europe. The musician says the move is made necessary by work, which is available in Europe, and the final wish of his dying mother who encouraged im to make the move. Page 1.

An Age-AGB McNair survey of 1,000 women over 18 has found that the average Melbourne woman feels good about her body, is not hung up about fashion and has a fondness for a god and for feminism. Over 80 percent of those surveyed believed a woman should no have to deal with harassment in the workplace. Page 1.

The Opposition, unions, youth and welfare groups have joined in condemning Prime Minister John Howard's plans for a trial work-for-dole scheme. The scheme, which would see unemployed 16 to 20-year-olds work up to 20 hours a week on community-based projects, has been labelled as piecemeal and unworkable by the plans' opponents. Page 1.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 937301800
